questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of using own funds?
o: Limited capacity to raise large amounts, plus opportunity cost
They must be repaid with interest
There are legal consequences if you default
questions.d: Own funds: capital from personal or internal sources (savings, asset sales, shares, retained profits). Advantage: no repayment or interest. Disadvantages: limited capacity, opportunity cost, less flexibility.
questions.w: Repayment with interest, default consequences and loan agreements all belong to borrowed funds.

questions.q: A medium-term loan lasts:
o: Over one year up to five years
questions.d: Loan term classification: short-term up to one year; medium-term over one year to five years; long-term over five years.
questions.w: Medium-term sits between short (≤1 year) and long (>5 years).

questions.q: What is the first step when taking out a loan?
o: Determine your creditworthiness by checking your credit score and history
questions.d: Loan steps: determine creditworthiness → research loan options → choose a lender → complete the application → wait for approval → receive funds → review terms.
questions.w: Your credit score affects whether you qualify and what rate you get, so it comes first.

questions.q: Which is a DISADVANTAGE of financing through a loan?
o: Collateral such as a house or car can be at risk if you cannot pay
Loans come in many types and terms
Loans give access to funds you would not otherwise have
questions.d: Disadvantages of loans: interest and fees, risk of default, potential for debt, collateral requirements.
questions.w: Predictable payments, flexibility and access to funds are advantages.

questions.q: Rashid borrows RO 4,000 for 5 years at 5% simple interest. What is the total amount he repays?
questions.d: Amount paid = Principal + Interest = P(1 + rt).

questions.q: The same RO 4,000 loan for 5 years is charged 5% compounded annually. How much interest does Rashid pay?
questions.d: Compound interest on a loan: I = P(1 + r)^t − P.
questions.w: 4,000 × 1.05^5 = RO 5,105.126, so interest = RO 1,105.126. It is more than the simple interest of RO 1,000.

questions.q: You need a RO 5,000 loan for 4 years. Most banks charge 5% compounded monthly; one bank charges 5.25% simple interest. Which is cheaper for YOU as the borrower?
o: It depends on the down payment
questions.d: As a borrower you want the option with the LOWER total interest.
questions.w: Compound: 5,000 × [(1 + 0.05/12)^48 − 1] = RO 1,104.477. Simple: 5,000 × 0.0525 × 4 = RO 1,050.000. The simple interest loan costs less.

questions.q: Sajid buys a RO 10,000 car, pays RO 2,000 down and borrows the rest for 12 months at 5% compounded monthly. What is the total he pays for the car?
questions.d: Total paid = down payment + loan amount repaid (principal + interest).

questions.q: Ahmed borrows RO 5,000 at 6% simple interest for 10 months. How much interest does he pay?
questions.d: Simple interest: I = P × r × t, with t in years.

questions.q: Ashraf gets a RO 600 cash advance and must repay RO 645 fifteen days later. What simple interest rate is this (360-day year)?
questions.d: Rate from simple interest: r = I ÷ (P × t).
questions.w: I = 645 − 600 = 45. t = 15 ÷ 360. r = 45 ÷ (600 × 15/360) = 45 ÷ 25 = 1.8 = 180%. Short-term advances can be very expensive.

questions.q: How is the APR different from the interest rate?
o: APR includes all fees and charges, so it shows the true annual cost of borrowing
APR ignores fees and only counts interest
APR is always lower than the interest rate
questions.d: APR (annual percentage rate): the yearly cost of borrowing including interest and all fees and charges.
questions.w: The interest rate is only the cost of borrowing the money; the APR adds fees such as processing and closing costs.

questions.q: Aju borrows RO 4,000 at 5% simple interest for 2 years, with RO 200 closing costs. What is the APR?
questions.d: APR = [(Total cost of credit ÷ Loan amount) ÷ Loan term] × 100.

questions.q: Raja takes a RO 100,000 mortgage for 60 months at 7% simple interest, with a 1.5% insurance fee and RO 500 processing cost. What is the APR?
questions.d: APR = [(Total cost of credit ÷ Loan amount) ÷ Loan term] × 100.

questions.q: Total finance charge equals:
o: Total of all instalment payments − amount financed
questions.d: Total finance charge: total interest paid = (Instalment amount × number of instalments) − amount financed.
questions.w: Everything you pay in instalments above the amount borrowed is the cost of finance.

questions.q: Deferred payment price equals:
o: Total of all instalment payments + down payment
Total of all instalment payments − amount financed
questions.d: Deferred payment price: total of all instalment payments + down payment (or purchase price + total finance charge).
questions.w: It is the full price you end up paying when you buy now and pay later.

questions.q: Adil buys a RO 36,500 car, pays RO 12,000 down and RO 450 a month for 60 months. What is the total finance charge?
questions.d: Total finance charge = total instalments − amount financed.
questions.w: Amount financed = 36,500 − 12,000 = 24,500. Instalments = 450 × 60 = 27,000. Finance charge = 27,000 − 24,500 = RO 2,500.

questions.q: For the same car (RO 36,500, RO 12,000 down, RO 450 × 60), what is the deferred payment price?
questions.d: Deferred payment price = total instalments + down payment.

questions.q: Ahmed borrows RO 10,000 at 12% for 2 years. What is the EMI using the FLAT interest rate method?
questions.d: Flat rate EMI = P × (1 + rt) ÷ number of monthly instalments.

questions.q: Same loan (RO 10,000, 12%, 2 years). What is the EMI using the REDUCING BALANCE method?
questions.d: Reducing balance EMI = P × R × (1 + R)^N ÷ [(1 + R)^N − 1], with R = annual rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100.
questions.w: R = 0.01, N = 24. EMI = 10,000 × 0.01 × 1.01^24 ÷ (1.01^24 − 1) = RO 470.735 (about RO 471). It is lower than the flat rate EMI.

questions.q: Which EMI method charges interest on the FULL original principal for the whole loan term?
questions.d: Flat rate method: interest is calculated on the original principal for the entire term and divided equally among the instalments.
questions.w: The reducing balance method charges interest only on the outstanding (unpaid) principal, which shrinks each month.

questions.q: Under the reducing balance method, as the loan goes on:
o: The interest part falls and the principal part rises
The interest part rises and the principal part falls
questions.d: Reducing balance: each EMI = interest on the outstanding principal + repayment of principal. The EMI stays the same.
questions.w: As the outstanding balance falls, the interest on it falls, so more of the fixed EMI goes to principal.

questions.q: Which Excel function gives the INTEREST part of a specific instalment?
questions.d: PMT: total payment per period. IPMT: interest part for a given period. PPMT: principal part for a given period. NPER: number of periods.
questions.w: The 'I' in IPMT stands for interest.

questions.q: Excel's RATE function returns a MONTHLY rate for a monthly loan. How do you get the annual rate?
questions.d: RATE(nper, pmt, pv, [fv], [type]) returns the interest rate per period.
questions.w: With monthly instalments the period is a month, so annual rate = monthly rate × 12 (and × 100 for a percentage).

questions.q: Secured loans require collateral such as a house or car.
questions.d: Secured loans require collateral; unsecured loans do not.
questions.w: Collateral is what makes the loan 'secured' for the lender.

questions.q: When an EMI is rounded, it is rounded down and the difference is added to the first instalment.
questions.d: Rounding an EMI is only for convenience of payment.
questions.w: It is always rounded UP, and the excess is adjusted in the LAST instalment, which ends up slightly lower.

questions.q: Ali borrows RO 1,200 at 12% p.a. to repay in 4 months. Find the EMI by (a) the reducing balance method and (b) the flat interest rate method, and show the reducing balance amortisation table.
questions.a:
(a) R = 0.12/12 = 0.01, N = 4
EMI = 1,200 × 0.01 × 1.01^4 ÷ (1.01^4 − 1) = RO 307.537
(b) Flat EMI = 1,200 × (1 + 0.12 × 4/12) ÷ 4 = 1,248 ÷ 4 = RO 312.000

Reducing balance table:
Month 1: interest RO 12.000, principal RO 295.537, balance RO 904.463
Month 2: interest RO 9.045, principal RO 298.493, balance RO 605.970
Month 3: interest RO 6.060, principal RO 301.478, balance RO 304.492
Month 4: interest RO 3.045, principal RO 304.492, balance RO 0.000
questions.d: EMI (equated monthly instalment): an equal monthly payment that covers interest and principal.
questions.w: In the reducing balance method interest falls each month because it is charged only on the outstanding balance, so the total cost is lower than the flat method.

questions.q: Rahima buys furniture worth RO 15,000, pays 20% down, and repays the rest in 15 equal monthly instalments at 6%. Find the EMI by (a) reducing balance and (b) flat rate.
questions.d: Flat EMI = P(1 + rt) ÷ N. Reducing balance EMI = P × R × (1 + R)^N ÷ [(1 + R)^N − 1].
questions.w: Only the amount borrowed (after the down payment) is financed, so start by subtracting the 20% down payment.

questions.q: A product costs RO 22,500. The buyer pays RO 6,000 down and 60 monthly payments of RO 310. Find the amount financed, total monthly payments, total finance charge, APR and deferred payment price.
questions.a:
Amount financed = 22,500 − 6,000 = RO 16,500
Total monthly payments = 310 × 60 = RO 18,600
Total finance charge = 18,600 − 16,500 = RO 2,100
APR = (2,100 ÷ 16,500) ÷ 5 × 100 = 2.55%
Deferred payment price = 18,600 + 6,000 = RO 24,600
questions.d: Amount financed = price − down payment. Finance charge = total instalments − amount financed. APR = (cost of credit ÷ loan) ÷ years × 100.
questions.w: The loan term is 60 months = 5 years, so divide by 5 in the APR formula.

questions.q: Adil buys a Land Rover for RO 36,500, pays RO 12,000 down and RO 450 per month for 60 months. Find (a) amount financed, (b) total finance charge, (c) APR, (d) deferred payment price.
questions.a:
(a) Amount financed = 36,500 − 12,000 = RO 24,500
(b) Total instalments = 450 × 60 = 27,000; finance charge = 27,000 − 24,500 = RO 2,500
(c) APR = (2,500 ÷ 24,500) ÷ 5 × 100 = 2.04%
(d) Deferred payment price = 27,000 + 12,000 = RO 39,000
questions.d: Deferred payment price: total of all instalments + down payment.
questions.w: Check: 36,500 purchase price + 2,500 finance charge also gives 39,000.

questions.q: Explain the difference between the flat interest rate method and the reducing balance method for EMIs, using a RO 10,000 loan at 12% for 2 years.
questions.a:
Flat rate: interest is charged on the full principal for the whole term. EMI = 10,000 × (1 + 0.12 × 2) ÷ 24 = RO 516.667 (≈ RO 517). Interest and principal parts stay the same every month.
Reducing balance: interest is charged only on the outstanding principal, compounded monthly. EMI = 10,000 × 0.01 × 1.01^24 ÷ (1.01^24 − 1) = RO 470.735 (≈ RO 471). Interest falls and principal repayment rises over time.
The reducing balance method is cheaper for the borrower and more accurate, and it is the most widely used.
questions.d: Reducing balance method: the most widely used EMI method; interest is calculated on the unpaid balance each month.
questions.w: The flat method keeps charging interest on money already repaid, so its EMI is higher.

questions.q: Find the EMI by the reducing balance method for RO 10,000 at 12% p.a. repaid in 4 equal monthly instalments, and show the amortisation table.
questions.a:
R = 0.01, N = 4
EMI = 10,000 × 0.01 × 1.01^4 ÷ (1.01^4 − 1) = RO 2,562.811

Month 1: interest RO 100.000, principal RO 2,462.811, balance RO 7,537.189
Month 2: interest RO 75.372, principal RO 2,487.439, balance RO 5,049.750
Month 3: interest RO 50.498, principal RO 2,512.313, balance RO 2,537.437
Month 4: interest RO 25.374, principal RO 2,537.437, balance RO 0.000
questions.d: Amortisation table: shows each payment split into interest and principal, and the remaining balance.
questions.w: Interest each month = outstanding balance × 1%. The rest of the EMI reduces the balance, which reaches zero after the 4th payment.
